learn.hook: A neem leaf is a solar-powered kitchen, and your gut is a 'food factory' with its own conveyor belt!
points: Autotrophs make their own food. In photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → (chlorophyll, sunlight) → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O. Extra carbohydrate is stored as starch.

Photosynthesis involves: light absorbed by chlorophyll; light energy changed to chemical energy and water split into hydrogen and oxygen; carbon dioxide reduced to carbohydrates. Gases pass through stomata, opened and closed by guard cells.

Heterotrophs depend on others: Amoeba engulfs food using pseudopodia into a food vacuole; fungi like bread mould break down food outside the body; parasites such as Cuscuta (amarbel), lice and tapeworms feed on a host.
Human digestion: saliva's salivary amylase breaks starch into sugar; the stomach's gastric glands release HCl (acidic medium), pepsin (digests proteins) and mucus (protects the lining).

In the small intestine, bile from the liver makes the food alkaline and emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice has trypsin (proteins) and lipase (fats); intestinal juice completes digestion to glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol. Villi absorb the food; the large intestine absorbs water.

example.q: Think it through: a variegated (green-and-white) money-plant leaf is kept in sunlight, then tested with iodine. Which parts turn blue-black?
steps: Starch is made by photosynthesis, which needs chlorophyll.
Only the green parts have chlorophyll.
example.answer: Only the parts that were green turn blue-black, showing chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

learn.reallife: A cow chewing grass for hours has a much longer small intestine than a tiger, because the cellulose in grass takes longer to digest than meat.

The journey of a roti
games.prompt: Follow the food through the alimentary canal

quiz.q: Which raw materials are needed for photosynthesis?
quiz.explain: Plants use carbon dioxide and water, with sunlight and chlorophyll, to make glucose and release oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Swaps raw materials and products

quiz.q: What opens and closes the stomata?
quiz.explain: Guard cells swell when water flows into them (pore opens) and shrink when they lose water (pore closes).
quiz.mistake: Does not know the role of guard cells

quiz.q: Desert plants keep stomata closed during the day. How do they get CO₂ for photosynthesis?
options: They do not photosynthesise at all
They take in CO₂ at night and store it as an intermediate for daytime use
quiz.explain: Opening stomata at night reduces water loss; the stored CO₂ is used when sunlight is available.
quiz.mistake: Thinks photosynthesis needs open stomata at the same moment

quiz.q: Which enzyme in saliva begins the digestion of starch?
quiz.explain: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into sugar in the mouth.
quiz.mistake: Confuses enzymes of mouth, stomach and intestine

quiz.q: What is the role of mucus in the stomach?
options: Protects the inner lining from acid
quiz.explain: Mucus protects the stomach lining from being damaged by hydrochloric acid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks mucus is a digestive enzyme

quiz.q: Bile juice does NOT contain enzymes, yet it helps digestion. How?
options: It breaks proteins into amino acids
It emulsifies large fat globules into smaller ones and makes the medium alkaline
quiz.explain: Bile salts break fats into small droplets so lipase can act, and bile neutralises the acidic food from the stomach.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every digestive juice must contain an enzyme

quiz.q: Why is the inner lining of the small intestine covered with villi?
options: To increase the surface area for absorption
quiz.explain: Finger-like villi greatly increase the absorbing surface and are richly supplied with blood vessels.
quiz.mistake: Thinks villi digest food mechanically

quiz.q: Cuscuta (amarbel) growing on other plants is an example of —
quiz.explain: Cuscuta draws its food from the host plant it grows on, so it is a parasite.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every plant must be autotrophic

teach.ask: Gappu munches a roti and asks: 'Where does my food go and how does it become small enough to enter my blood?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Enzymes break it down and the villi in the small intestine absorb it. My roti is now energy!
teach.nudge: Good! But which part of the gut absorbs the digested food, and with what?

learn.hook: Every breath you take helps your cells 'burn' glucose without a single flame!
points: Respiration releases energy from food. First, glucose (6 carbons) is broken into pyruvate (3 carbons) in the cytoplasm.
Without oxygen: in yeast, pyruvate becomes ethanol + CO₂ (fermentation); in our muscles during hard exercise it becomes lactic acid, causing cramps.
With oxygen (aerobic), in the mitochondria, pyruvate is broken into CO₂ and water, releasing much more energy. Energy is stored as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Air path: nostrils (hairs and mucus filter dust) → throat → trachea (rings of cartilage stop it collapsing) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli, where gases are exchanged with blood.

Breathing in: ribs lift and the diaphragm flattens, making the chest cavity larger. Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen; CO₂ is more soluble in water and is carried mostly dissolved in blood. Aquatic animals breathe faster because water has less dissolved oxygen.

example.q: Think it through: why do your legs ache with cramps after a fast 400 m race on Sports Day?
steps: During a sprint muscles need energy faster than oxygen can reach them.
Muscle cells then break pyruvate without oxygen.
This produces lactic acid, which builds up and causes cramps.
example.answer: Lactic acid builds up from anaerobic respiration in muscles when oxygen runs short.

learn.reallife: Idli and dosa batter rises overnight because yeast and bacteria respire anaerobically, releasing carbon dioxide that makes it fluffy.

games.title: The path of air into the lungs

quiz.q: Where does the first step of breaking glucose into pyruvate take place?
quiz.explain: Glucose is split into pyruvate in the cytoplasm; further aerobic breakdown happens in the mitochondria.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all of respiration happens inside mitochondria

quiz.q: How many carbon atoms does a pyruvate molecule have?
quiz.explain: One 6-carbon glucose splits into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules.
quiz.mistake: Gives the carbon count of glucose

quiz.q: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
quiz.explain: Yeast ferments pyruvate into ethanol and CO₂ without oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up yeast with muscle cells

quiz.q: Why do the walls of the trachea have rings of cartilage?
options: To make sure the air passage does not collapse
quiz.explain: Cartilage rings keep the trachea open so air can always flow.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the job of cartilage with hairs and mucus

quiz.q: Which molecule is called the energy currency of the cell?
quiz.explain: Energy released in respiration is stored in ATP and used for cell activities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks glucose itself is used directly as the cell's energy currency

quiz.q: Why do fish breathe much faster than land animals?
options: The amount of oxygen dissolved in water is much lower than in air
quiz.explain: Dissolved oxygen in water is low, so aquatic animals must move water over gills quickly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks water contains more oxygen because H₂O has oxygen

quiz.q: What happens during inhalation (breathing in)?
options: Ribs lift and the diaphragm flattens, enlarging the chest cavity
Ribs move down and the diaphragm curves upward
quiz.explain: A bigger chest cavity lowers the pressure inside, so air rushes into the lungs.
quiz.mistake: Reverses inhalation and exhalation

quiz.q: Which pigment carries oxygen in human blood?
quiz.explain: Haemoglobin in red blood cells has a very high affinity for oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a blood pigment with a plant pigment

teach.ask: Gappu pants after flying: 'Why do I breathe faster when I fly fast? What do my cells do with oxygen?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Cells use oxygen to break glucose into carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy as ATP!
teach.nudge: Nice try! What do cells break down with oxygen, and what do they get from it?

learn.hook: Your heart is a four-room pump that keeps beating your whole life without a single holiday!
points: Blood has plasma (carries food, CO₂ and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form), red blood cells (carry oxygen) and platelets (help blood clot to stop bleeding).

The human heart has four chambers. Right side: deoxygenated blood from the body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs. Left side: oxygenated blood from the lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → whole body. Valves stop backflow.

Blood passes through the heart twice per cycle (double circulation), keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate. Fish have a two-chambered heart; amphibians and many reptiles have three chambers.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls; veins bring blood back, have thinner walls and valves; capillaries are one cell thick. Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm of Hg, measured with a sphygmomanometer. Lymph carries digested fat from the intestine and drains extra tissue fluid back into blood.

Plants: xylem carries water and minerals up from roots, pulled mainly by transpiration (evaporation of water from leaves) during the day; root pressure helps at night. Phloem carries food such as sucrose in both directions (translocation), using energy from ATP.

example.q: Think it through: why do the ventricles have thicker muscular walls than the atria?
steps: Atria only push blood a short distance, into the ventricles.
Ventricles pump blood out to the lungs and to the whole body.
That needs much more force, so they need thicker muscles.
example.answer: Ventricles must pump blood to distant organs, so they need thicker, stronger walls.

learn.reallife: When a doctor wraps a cuff around your arm and pumps it up, she is measuring your blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer.

games.title: Path of blood through the heart
games.prompt: Starting from blood returning from the body

games.title: Match the part to its job
pairs: Carries blood away from the heart

quiz.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
quiz.explain: The human heart has two atria and two ventricles — four chambers.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the human heart with that of fish or amphibians

quiz.q: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body?
quiz.explain: The left ventricle receives oxygen-rich blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up left and right sides

quiz.q: Why is separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood useful for birds and mammals?
options: It gives a highly efficient oxygen supply needed to keep a constant body temperature
It removes the need for lungs
quiz.explain: Birds and mammals use a lot of energy to maintain body temperature, so they need efficient oxygen delivery.
quiz.mistake: Does not link double circulation to high energy needs

quiz.q: What is the main force that pulls water up through the xylem of a tall tree during the day?
quiz.explain: Evaporation of water from leaves creates a suction that pulls water up the xylem.
quiz.mistake: Thinks root pressure alone lifts water during the day

quiz.q: Which blood vessels have valves to prevent the backflow of blood?
quiz.explain: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so valves keep it flowing towards the heart.
quiz.mistake: Thinks arteries have valves along their length

quiz.q: What does lymph do?
options: Carries digested and absorbed fat and drains extra tissue fluid back into blood
quiz.explain: Lymph collects fluid that leaks out of capillaries and carries absorbed fat from the intestine.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lymph with blood

quiz.q: Translocation in plants refers to —
quiz.explain: Translocation is the movement of soluble products of photosynthesis through phloem, using energy from ATP.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the jobs of xylem and phloem

quiz.q: Which part of blood helps stop bleeding from a cut?
quiz.explain: Platelets help blood to clot at the site of injury.
quiz.mistake: Thinks red blood cells clot blood

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does oxygen from my lungs reach my toes? Explain my heart's pumping!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood through arteries, and veins bring it back — round and round!
teach.nudge: Good start! Which side of the heart sends oxygen-rich blood to the body?

learn.hook: Your two bean-shaped kidneys filter your blood all day — like a super-careful water purifier!
points: Excretion removes harmful nitrogenous wastes such as urea. The human excretory system: a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and the urethra.
Each kidney has many filtering units called nephrons. In each nephron, a cluster of capillaries (glomerulus) sits inside a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule, where blood is filtered.
As the filtrate passes along the tubule, useful substances like glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water are reabsorbed. The rest becomes urine, stored in the bladder.
If kidneys fail, an artificial kidney (haemodialysis) removes nitrogenous wastes from the blood by passing it through a dialysing fluid, but it does not reabsorb anything.
Plants excrete oxygen and water vapour through stomata, store wastes in vacuoles and in leaves that fall off, and store some wastes as resins and gums in old xylem.

example.q: Think it through: about 180 litres of filtrate is formed in the kidneys every day, but only a litre or two of urine is passed. Where does the rest go?
steps: The filtrate contains water, glucose, amino acids and salts along with urea.
Tubules of the nephron reabsorb useful substances and most of the water.
So only a small volume, rich in wastes, leaves as urine.
example.answer: Most of it is reabsorbed back into the blood by the kidney tubules.

learn.reallife: The dark sticky resin oozing from a pine (chir) tree or the gum on a babool tree is partly how plants store their waste products.

items.text: The filtering unit of the kidney is the ___.
The cluster of capillaries in Bowman's capsule is the ___.
Urine passes from each kidney to the bladder through the ___.
A machine used when kidneys fail is an artificial kidney, used in ___.
Plants store some wastes as resins and gums in old ___.

items.q: Main nitrogenous waste in human urine?
Number of kidneys in a human?
Tube carrying urine out of the body?
Gas plants release by day through stomata?

quiz.q: What is the basic filtering unit of the kidney?
quiz.explain: Each kidney contains a large number of nephrons that filter the blood.
quiz.mistake: Confuses nephron with neuron

quiz.q: What is reabsorbed from the filtrate as it moves along the tubule?
options: Glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water
quiz.explain: Useful substances return to the blood; wastes stay behind to form urine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the filtrate is passed out unchanged

quiz.q: Which is the correct path of urine?
quiz.explain: Urine forms in the kidney, travels down the ureter, is stored in the bladder and leaves through the urethra.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ureter and urethra

quiz.q: How does haemodialysis differ from a real kidney?
options: It filters blood but does not reabsorb useful substances
It is done by the lungs
quiz.explain: The artificial kidney only removes wastes through a dialysing fluid; there is no reabsorption.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a dialysis machine copies every kidney function

quiz.q: Where does blood get filtered in a nephron?
options: In the glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule
quiz.explain: The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries; filtration happens into the surrounding Bowman's capsule.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the bladder filters urine

quiz.q: Which is NOT a way plants get rid of wastes?
options: Storing gums and resins in old xylem
quiz.explain: Plants have no excretory organs like a bladder; they use leaves, vacuoles, gums, resins and stomata.
quiz.mistake: Assumes plants have organs like animals

quiz.q: The main nitrogenous waste removed by human kidneys is —
quiz.explain: Urea, a nitrogen-containing waste, is removed in urine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks glucose is a waste

quiz.q: The amount of water reabsorbed in the kidneys depends on —
options: The amount of oxygen in air
How much excess water the body has and how much waste needs to be dissolved
quiz.explain: The body adjusts reabsorption to keep its water balance, so urine volume changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reabsorption is always fixed

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does pee come from? How do my kidneys clean my blood?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Nephrons filter the blood, take back the good stuff, and the waste goes out as urine!
teach.nudge: Good! What useful things do the kidneys take back before making urine?
